title: Encoded Polyline Decoder: String to Coordinates
description: Decode Google's encoded polyline strings back to coordinates with the Encoded Polyline Decoder — the algorithm's own test string verified. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Google’s canonical test string _p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC_mqNvxq`@ decodes to (38.5, −120.2), (40.7, −120.95) and (43.252, −126.453) — the three points from the format’s own documentation.
quick_answer: The Encoded Polyline Decoder turns encoded polyline strings — the compressed coordinate format Google’s APIs return for routes — back into latitude/longitude pairs. Paste the string and read the points: the binary-delta encoding undone step by step, in your browser, at the standard precision of five decimal places.

body.t: The directions API returned a string; your map drew it in the wrong ocean. Decode it here and read the actual points — the bug is usually precision or a lat/lon flip. The reverse craft is the
Old logs and URLs carry polylines long after the originals vanished. Decoding resurrects the geometry as coordinates any tool here can use.
Decode the canonical example, change one character, decode again — the delta encoding’s behaviour teaches itself faster than any spec.
Decoded pairs paste into distance, mapping and conversion tools. The string was a container; the points are the content.

_p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC_mqNvxq`@ is the worked example from Google’s own documentation, decoding to the three California-to-Oregon points (38.5, −120.2), (40.7, −120.95), (43.252, −126.453). Any decoder that cannot reproduce these is not a decoder.

Polylines are delta chains: corrupt one character early and every later point shifts. A route that starts right and wanders increasingly wrong has a mid-string wound — decoding exposes where sanity ends.

popular_table.title: How the encoding works
rows: Each value stored as the difference from the previous one
Negatives transformed (left-shift, invert) so small numbers stay small
Values split into 5-bit chunks, +63, printed as ASCII characters
popular_table.note: Precision 5 is the Google standard; some libraries (OSRM, Mapbox options) use precision 6. A string decoded at the wrong precision yields points 10× too near the equator/prime meridian — the classic symptom.

faq: Five decimal places — the original Google format. Strings from precision-6 systems need a decoder set to 6; the symptom of a mismatch is unmistakable (points huddle near 0,0 scaled wrong).
Decoding produces the coordinate list — paste the points into mapping tools to draw. This page’s craft is the faithful expansion of the string.
The standard format encodes latitude/longitude only. Some extensions smuggle altitude as a third value per point — those are non-standard dialects, flagged when they appear.
Why does my string start with letters like ‘o’ or ‘_’?
The characters are ASCII 63–126 — punctuation and lowercase letters mostly. A string starting ‘_p~iF’ is geography’s most famous fingerprint (the canonical example).
A string cut mid-value decodes a partial final point or fails — the decoder reports what decoded cleanly rather than inventing a tail.
Is it the same as a geohash?
No — geohashes name single cells; polylines encode sequences of points. Both compress coordinates into strings, for opposite jobs.
A related but different format (variable precision, third dimension support). It needs its own decoder — do not feed it here and blame the string.
